reading.title: City Park Volunteers: A Flexible Evening and Weekend Schedule
reading.focus: Understanding schedules, roles, and comparisons in a community programme
reading.passage: Maplewood City Park relies on local volunteers to keep its gardens, paths, and playgrounds welcoming. Last year, the council introduced a new volunteer schedule to attract people who work or study during the day. Instead of only morning shifts, the park now offers evening sessions on weekdays and longer sessions at weekends. The change increased regular volunteers from 40 to 95 in eight months. The coordinator, Dana Ellis, says the main reason for the growth is flexibility, not advertising. People can choose short tasks after work or join a full weekend team. This claim is supported by signup data: over 70% of new volunteers selected evening or weekend slots because they could not attend mornings. The weekly schedule is organised around three roles. Garden helpers water plants, plant flowers, and collect fallen leaves. Path monitors walk the main trails, report damage, and help visitors with directions. Play assistants stay near the playground, tidy equipment, and organise simple games for children on Saturday afternoons. Volunteers choose one main role each month but may try another role if spaces allow. Evening shifts run on Tuesdays and Thursdays from 6 p.m. to 7.30 p.m. These shifts focus on light work such as watering, litter collection, and sweeping entrances. Weekend shifts are longer. On Saturdays, volunteers work from 9 a.m. to 12 p.m., with a break for drinks provided by the park café. On Sundays, there is a shorter tidy-up session from 10 a.m. to 11.30 a.m. The park provides gloves, tools, and training, so no experience is needed. For example, new garden helpers attend a 30-minute introduction on how to use tools safely and how to identify weeds. This example shows the type of support offered, but it does not mean all roles need the same training. Path monitors, for instance, receive a map and a short briefing rather than tool training. The schedule also includes a monthly evening meeting on the first Wednesday from 7 p.m. to 8 p.m. Volunteers review progress, suggest improvements, and plan seasonal events such as the autumn tree-planting day. Attendance is encouraged but not required. Compared with the old morning-only system, the new system asks for fewer hours per person but involves more people overall. The council believes this shared approach reduces pressure and builds community. Many volunteers also say they enjoy meeting neighbours and learning simple gardening skills during these relaxed sessions. Early results suggest fewer missed shifts and cleaner public areas, although a full review will be published next spring.

exercises.focus: Understanding schedules, roles, and comparisons in a community programme
exercises.passage: Maplewood City Park relies on local volunteers to keep its gardens, paths, and playgrounds welcoming. Last year, the council introduced a new volunteer schedule to attract people who work or study during the day. Volunteers choose one main role each month but may try another role if spaces allow. Evening shifts run on Tuesdays and Thursdays from 6 p.m. to 7.30 p.m. These shifts focus on light work such as watering, litter collection, and sweeping entrances. Weekend shifts are longer. On Saturdays, volunteers work from 9 a.m. to 12 p.m., with a break for drinks provided by the park café. On Sundays, there is a shorter tidy-up session from 10 a.m. to 11.30 a.m. The park provides gloves, tools, and training, so no experience is needed. For example, new garden helpers attend a 30-minute introduction on how to use tools safely and how to identify weeds. This example shows the type of support offered, but it does not mean all roles need the same training. Path monitors, for instance, receive a map and a short briefing rather than tool training. The schedule also includes a monthly evening meeting on the first Wednesday from 7 p.m. to 8 p.m. Volunteers review progress, suggest improvements, and plan seasonal events such as the autumn tree-planting day. Attendance is encouraged but not required. Compared with the old morning-only system, the new system asks for fewer hours per person but involves more people overall. The council believes this shared approach reduces pressure and builds community. Many volunteers also say they enjoy meeting neighbours and learning simple gardening skills during these relaxed sessions. Total visitors: 2023: 395, 2024: 470.

writingPrompts.task: Task 2 · School Visits to Local Museums
writingPrompts.focus: evaluation of linked ideas with clear comparison
writingPrompts.prompt: Some schools organise regular workshops at local museums, while other schools prefer classroom activities only. Do the advantages of museum workshops outweigh the disadvantages? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own experience. Write at least 250 words in about 40 minutes.

speakingPrompts.focus: paraphrase of familiar questions with linked answers
speakingPrompts.prompt: Let's talk about your studies and free time. What subject are you studying at the moment? What do you enjoy most about it? How do you usually spend your weekends? Have your leisure activities changed compared to last year? Do you prefer spending free time indoors or outdoors? Why? This part takes 4 to 5 minutes.

speakingPrompts.focus: corrected details in short personal answers
speakingPrompts.prompt: Let's talk about gardens and your local area. Is there a park or garden near where you live? How often do you visit it? Did you enjoy gardening or outdoor activities as a child? Would you like to join a community garden open day in the future? Why or why not? This part takes 4 to 5 minutes.

speakingPrompts.task: Part 2 · Cue card – A Useful Talk or Panel You Attended
speakingPrompts.focus: linked ideas in a 1 to 2 minute talk
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Describe a useful talk or panel discussion you attended at school, university, or in your community. You should say:
• where and when it took place
• who the speakers were
• what main ideas they shared
• explain why you found it useful
You have 1 minute to prepare and should speak for 1 to 2 minutes. Possible follow-up: Would you attend a similar event again?

speakingPrompts.task: Part 3 · Careers Advice for Young People
speakingPrompts.focus: reasons and evaluation, not memorised facts
speakingPrompts.prompt: Let's discuss careers advice. Why do some students find a university careers panel more helpful than reading online? How can schools help students compare different job options clearly? Do you think work experience is more important than careers talks? Why? How might careers advice change in the next ten years? This discussion takes 4 to 5 minutes.

speakingPrompts.focus: comparison and evaluation of community activities
speakingPrompts.prompt: Let's discuss museums and community learning. What are the benefits of local museum workshops compared to learning at home? Should museums offer more free activities for families? Why? How can a community garden open day and a museum workshop both support local learning? Which is more important for a town: preserving old objects or creating new green spaces? Why? This discussion takes 4 to 5 minutes.
